justice: The street allocates substantial width to motor vehicles, with multiple parked cars occupying both sides of the carriageway, while the pedestrian zone on the shop side is comparatively narrow.

A raised sidewalk exists along the building frontage, which provides some dedicated pedestrian space, but the usable width is reduced by storefront edges, utility items, and small objects near the curb.
No visible tactile paving, marked curb ramps, or other universal-design elements can be identified, limiting accessibility for users with diverse mobility or sensory needs.
safety: Parallel parked cars line the roadway and narrow the effective travel space, increasing dooring and maneuvering conflicts among drivers, pedestrians, and any cyclists.
There is no visible marked crosswalk, traffic-calming feature, or protected pedestrian crossing in the scene, which weakens protection for people moving between the shop side and the tree-lined side.
Daytime visibility is good because of open sightlines and bright weather, but the long shared vehicular surface still appears dominated by cars rather than clearly separated user zones.
livability: Ground-floor commercial storefronts on the right suggest access to daily services and some degree of street activity.
The tree-lined edge on the left adds greenery and creates a more pleasant public-realm backdrop than a fully paved street.
However, the street appears dominated by parked vehicles and hard paving, which reduces space for lingering, social use, and everyday public life.
sustainability: Rows of mature trees on the left provide ecological value, shade, and some mitigation of heat and air-quality impacts.
The street lacks visible bicycle facilities or dedicated transit infrastructure in the frame, so support for low-carbon travel modes appears limited.
Large paved roadway and parking surfaces indicate a car-oriented allocation of space, which is less supportive of sustainable streetscape design.
aesthetics: The continuous row of trees on the left contributes visual softness and balances the built form.
The commercial building frontage on the right has a relatively coherent massing, but the varied signage and parked cars create a cluttered visual impression at street level.
The street appears generally clean and orderly, yet the broad asphalt surface and vehicle presence make the scene feel more utilitarian than scenic.
comfort: Thermal comfort is uneven: the left side benefits from substantial tree shade, while the right-side sidewalk and roadway are exposed to strong direct sun.
Physical comfort for walking is moderate because there is a raised sidewalk, but its width appears limited and interrupted by curbside objects and frontage conditions.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the dominance of parked and moving vehicles in close proximity to pedestrian space, making the environment feel more traffic-oriented than relaxed.
walkability: A continuous sidewalk is present along the building side, which supports basic pedestrian movement.
Walkability is weakened by the narrowness of the pedestrian zone compared with the roadway and by the absence of visible crossing markings or pedestrian-priority features.
Shade from the tree row improves comfort on the left side of the street environment, but the main walking edge next to the shops appears sunnier and less protected.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, cycle track, or visible bicycle markings can be identified in the roadway.
Parked cars along both sides create potential dooring hazards and leave limited comfortable space for on-street cycling.
There is no visible bicycle parking, intersection treatment, or separation from motor traffic, making the street poorly equipped for everyday cycling.
